summary: This RFC points out three errors in the Military Standard Transmission Control Protocol (MIL-STD-1778) and proposes solutions, to help implementers get a reliable implementation.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone reads the military's rule book for TCP, spots three mistakes, and suggests fixes.

what errors are in the military standard tcp
why does syn data get rejected in mil-std tcp
subtitle: Three errors found in the Military Standard TCP specification, with proposed fixes.

tldr.problem: The Military Standard TCP (MIL-STD-1778, dated August 1983) contains specification errors that stop a faithful implementation from working properly.
tldr.mechanism: The authors trace the three-way handshake and data reception step by step, locate three faults, and propose a fix for each.
tldr.outcome: The errors were submitted to DCA and were to be corrected in the next update of the MIL STD TCP specification. Implementers were told to include the corrections.

today: RFC 964 is an Informational note from November 1985 and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It describes errors in the Military Standard TCP, not in the Internet's RFC 793, and says the errors were to be corrected in the next update of the military standard.

sections.title: Why the Standard Was Checked
sections.content:
Sidhu and Blumer were preparing to verify the connection management of the Military Standard Transmission Control Protocol (MIL-STD-1778, 12 August 1983). While studying it, they noticed several errors. As a result, TCP entities following the specification would not receive data in the SYN_RECVD and ESTAB states.

The authors had earlier verified the NBS class 4 transport protocol (TP4) with a software tool. That work found incompleteness errors but no deadlocks or livelocks. TCP, the RFC reminds readers, is a transport-level connection-oriented protocol offering reliable, ordered delivery over full-duplex, flow-controlled virtual connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Before testing a game's rules properly, someone read them closely and found spots where the game would get stuck.

sections.title: Problem 1: Data That Arrives With a SYN
sections.content:
In the three-way handshake, entity A sends a SYN (here with data), B answers with a SYN ACK, and A sends an ACK. Five state transitions and three segments are involved in the simplest case.

The fault is in how record_syn and accept_policy interact. record_syn updates recv_next before it calls accept_policy. By then recv_next is greater than seg.seq_num, so neither acceptance strategy in accept_policy works, and the data is wrongly rejected.

The proposed fix is to have record_syn call accept_policy before recv_next is updated.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like updating the page counter before checking which page you were on, so you decide the page you just got does not belong.

sections.title: Problem 2: No Timer for the First SYN
sections.content:
The Active Open actions, with or without data, call open and gen_syn. Neither sets a retransmission timer. If the initial SYN is lost, no timer expires, so the SYN is never resent and the connection cannot be established.

This differs from sending data in the ESTAB state, where dispatch calls send_new_data, which does start a retransmission timer. The fix is to have gen_syn or open explicitly request the retransmission timer.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send an invitation but never set a reminder to check for a reply, a lost invitation means you wait forever.

sections.title: Problem 3: Data in the ESTAB State
sections.content:
When both entities are in ESTAB and one sends data, the receiver's actions are wrong. For the in-order, valid case the specification uses row 6 of the table, which calls update. That routine does nothing to accept the incoming data or pass it to the user. The accept action procedure must be called so data can be queued and possibly delivered.

The cause is apparently a transposition of the action tables on pages 111 and 112, which should be interchanged. That change also fixes a related problem: an entity could never reach the CLOSE_WAIT state from ESTAB.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail carrier arrives with a package but the house has no one assigned to take it inside, because two instruction pages were swapped.

sections.title: Consequences for Implementers
sections.content:
The authors also note general slips: several variable and procedure names are misspelled and the action statements are often syntactically incorrect, which an automatic syntax checker would have caught. That would be hard for this document because it is not based on a formalized description technique.

A faithful implementation of the standard would be unable to receive data sent with a SYN, to establish a connection if the first SYN is lost, or to receive data in ESTAB. An implementation therefore must include the corrections. The errors were submitted to DCA for the next update of the standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone building from these instructions must fix the mistakes first, or the finished machine will not work.
